rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A makes userUpdatePrisma hash any password passed to it. Change B's new userChangePassword controller already hashes the new password with hashPassword before calling userUpdatePrisma. After merging, the endpoint POST /api/user/password double-hashes: A's hashing is applied on top of B's already-hashed value. The stored value becomes hash(hash(newPassword)), so after a password change via the new endpoint, login with the new password fails (compareWithHash(newPassword, hash(hash(newPassword))) is false). B's own test only checks the stored password differs from plain text, so it still passes. This is a runtime conflict: each change is correct alone, but together the change-password flow locks users out. It also overlaps in intent, since both fix hashing on password updates at different layers.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A adds @updatedAt to Article.updatedAt so Prisma auto-bumps it on every update and removes the manual updatedAt set in articleUpdatePrisma. Change B adds a views counter incremented via prisma.article.update on every article GET. Combined, the @updatedAt attribute makes every view increment also bump Article.updatedAt, so merely reading an article changes its 'last updated' timestamp. Neither change alone does this: in B alone, updatedAt stays untouched by view increments; in A alone, only real edits bump it. The merged code therefore reports wrong updatedAt values in article responses (articleViewer likely exposes updatedAt) whenever someone reads an article, after the previous edit semantics. The article returned in the same request was fetched before the increment, but the next read shows a bumped updatedAt, and any ordering/caching by updatedAt is corrupted.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A switches the list ordering from updatedAt desc to createdAt desc. Change B adds an `after=<slug>` cursor that filters on `updatedAt < cursor.updatedAt` while relying on the list still being ordered by updatedAt desc. After merging, the list is sorted by createdAt but the cursor filters on updatedAt. If an article was edited, its updatedAt diverges from its createdAt order, so pagination with `after` skips or repeats articles. Example: articles X (created Jan 1), Y (created Jan 2), Z (created Jan 3); X is edited on Jan 10. The list order is Z, Y, X. With limit=1, after=Z gives updatedAt < Z.updatedAt (Jan 3), which excludes X (updated Jan 10), so the page returns Y. Then after=Y gives updatedAt < Jan 2, which returns nothing, so X is never reached. Each change passes alone, and the merged tests use unedited articles where the two timestamps agree, so they still pass.

rows.explanation: Change A switches the list ordering from updatedAt desc to createdAt desc so that editing an article no longer moves it up the list. Listing with limit=2 returns newer articles by createdAt, e.g. [three, two]; requesting after=two uses two.updatedAt, so the filter keeps only articles with updatedAt older than two, which silently skips the edited article X (whose updatedAt is now the newest) even though it sits next in createdAt order. Items can be skipped or duplicated in pagination. B's new test passes only because it never edits an article, so createdAt and updatedAt orderings coincide... (B's test pins updatedAt, but createdAt remains near-identical insertion order, so it passes by accident).

So every read of an article now changes its updatedAt timestamp, and the returned/stored updatedAt no longer reflects the last content edit. Neither change alone has this issue: A's @updatedAt only fires on real edits (before B), and B's increment doesn't touch updatedAt without @updatedAt. Merged, GET /articles/:slug (which returns the article, possibly fetched before the bump but stored value is wrong thereafter) and list/feed responses expose a wrong updatedAt that changes with page views. This is a concrete wrong behavior arising only from the combination; existing tests likely don't check updatedAt stability.

Because deleteMany on model Tag is in the WRITE_ACTIONS list and the model is Tag, A's middleware invalidates the cache after B's cleanup. The article.delete also invalidates the cache first, but the orphan cleanup runs afterward as a separate call, which also invalidates. A request that populates the cache between the article delete and the tag deleteMany could cache a stale list, but the subsequent deleteMany invalidation clears it after completion, so the final state is consistent. The tests do not conflict: A's tests do not delete articles, and B's test only checks the DB. The two changes address different problems and stay correct together.

Neither change alone behaves this way: before A, slugs never changed, so B's slug-keyed table was consistent. The merge works only because of A's slug change breaking B's assumption of slug stability (Comment has an FK with cascade for slugs, but RecentView does not).

rows.label: conflict

After merging, the list is ordered by createdAt desc but the cursor filters on updatedAt. Concrete scenario: article X is created first and later edited (updatedAt is now the newest); articles Y and Z are created afterwards. Order by createdAt desc is Z, Y, X. Requesting ?after=Y uses Y.updatedAt as the cutoff, and X (updatedAt newer than Y's) is excluded by the lt filter, so X, which should follow Y, is silently skipped. Conversely, pages can include items that were already shown. B's test sets only updatedAt and passes because creation order coincides with update order. The two changes make incompatible assumptions about what the sort key is.
